Overview

Social habit tracking for vapers, without the verdict

Role

UX research, information architecture, user flows, wireframes, visual design, interactive prototype, React front end

Team

Meisum · Hardware & Firmware
Caroline · Interface

Timeline

13 weeks · Jun 22 to Sep 20, 2026

Interface prototype is demo-ready. The hardware module is in calibration.

Tools

Figma, React + Vite, Claude Code, Web Bluetooth, Typeform

Exhale is a harm-reduction and awareness product, not a medical device, and it makes no clinical claims. Built for adults 21+.

Problem

Every vaping app I studied makes the same decision before you even open it: you are quitting. A counter starts, a quit date gets set, and every heavier day turns into a small confession to your phone. That works for people who are ready. It loses everyone else, and the research says everyone else is most people. Only about half of daily vapers intend to quit at all, and young adults, the fastest growing group, are the first to delete a tool that lectures them. On top of that, almost every tracker runs on manual logging, which is the first habit users drop.

Solution

Exhale pairs a small silicone module that clips onto the vape you already own with a companion app that behaves like a social platform instead of a clinic. The module logs every puff over Bluetooth with zero input. The app turns that data into a calm daily read and a friends-only space called a pod. At onboarding you choose a pathway: the red pill to quit or taper, or the blue pill to keep vaping and simply understand it. Both are equal, both are reversible, and both run on the same data.

Goal

Make people cognizant of their own patterns without stigma, and build a daily ritual strong enough to keep them opening the app whether or not they ever decide to quit.

01 · The brief

Red pill / blue pill

The brief I set for the team came straight from The Matrix. Take the red pill and you face the hard truth: you want to quit, and you want help doing it. Take the blue pill and you stay comfortable: you keep vaping, but you'd like to know what that actually looks like. Most products only sell the red pill and treat everyone else as a conversion they haven't made yet. We decided to sell both, and to make the blue pill a first-class choice instead of a failure state.

Red pill · Quit or taper

I want out.

For people ready to cut back. Taper schedules with decreasing daily limits, milestones, a forgiving streak that freezes instead of resetting to zero, and a pod that keeps them honest between Mondays. Encouraging, never preachy.

Blue pill · Keep vaping

I just want to know.

For people who aren't quitting and don't want to be told to. Neutral, data-forward numbers, a time-of-day heat map, real cost, and pods that stay optional. No nudges toward quitting, ever. The data does the talking.

Reverse color psychology

Why the colors are flipped

Red usually means stop, so we gave it to quitting on purpose. Red reads as the harder, taboo side, and blue reads as the comfortable one. Putting blue on the stay side lowers the stakes of opening the app at all, which matters more for retention than any single feature. It's a little cheeky, and that was the point.

One app, two lenses

Same data, different mode

Picking a pill doesn't create a second app. It flips a mode flag that re-skins a personalization layer, and you can switch any time from Profile. Data carries over. Everything structural stays shared.

02 · Research

Understanding the space

Market research

Who vapes, and how much

18 to 25

The highest-prevalence age band in every national survey we reviewed. SAMHSA puts 18 to 25 year olds at 23.7% in 2024, up from 11.7% in 2020.

48.5%

of daily exclusive vapers intend to quit at all, and most who do give themselves a year or more. The blue pill is the majority.

58.3%

of regular young vapers use every day. Daily vs. non-daily turned out to be the cleanest line between light and heavy use.

27%

of daily users vape within five minutes of waking, a classic dependence marker and exactly the kind of pattern a heat map makes visible.

Sources: NCHS Data Brief 475 (NHIS 2021); SAMHSA via Patton et al. 2026; Aherrera et al., Tobacco Induced Diseases 2020; Chaiton et al., Substance Abuse 2023. Research compiled by Adamaris. Survey methods differ, so we report ranges and name the source each time.

Competitive analysis

Nothing sat in the middle

We audited three camps. Quit apps like Puff Count, Quit Vaping, Quash and VapeFree track usage, but they run on manual logging and offer community that's wellness-only and shallow. Built-in trackers like Vuse Ultra and JUUL C1 log automatically, then lock you into one device and one closed app. Social platforms like BeReal and Strava own the rituals and the retention, with no tracking at all.

On hardware, Meisum found every built-in tracker is tied to its own device, and the only retrofit add-ons were an academic research platform and an abandoned LED-reading prototype. A small, universal, automatic add-on was open ground, which meant the interface had to carry the rest of the differentiation.

Pattern research

What we borrowed

BeReal

An unpredictable daily moment that's hard to fake. Became the Exhale.

Strava

Data as achievement, clubs, and leaderboards against your own past. Became pods and consistency ranking.

YikYak

Pseudonymity lowers the cost of honesty. Also our cautionary tale: anonymity without moderation turns toxic.

Oura

One summary ring up front, depth on demand. Became the calm ring and progressive disclosure into stats.

03 · Who it's for

Target audience

Our primary market is adults 21 to 25: college students and recent grads who already live on BeReal, TikTok and Instagram, and who expect a new app to feel familiar on the first tap. We set the minimum age at 21 to match the legal purchase age in most places, and the brand never markets nicotine or makes vaping look fun. Every screen had to pass one design filter: if a choice only works for one of these two people, it's the wrong choice.

21+ onlyCollege + recent gradsSocial-first, iOS-firstPseudonymous by default

"I'm not trying to quit. I just want to know my actual numbers."

  • IT support, stress vapes around the 2 to 5pm work crunch
  • Already tracks his steps, sleep and spending
  • Reads privacy policies. Will never post under his real name
Wants

Real usage, true monthly cost, insight over encouragement, control on his own terms.

Churns on

04 · Unique value proposition

The pitch

The only vape tracker that works on the vape you already own, and the only one your friends are actually in.

01

Zero-input tracking

A clip-on silicone module reads airflow on every draw and syncs over Bluetooth. There is no log button anywhere in the app. Manual logging, the top complaint across every quit app we reviewed, is designed out.

02

Friends-only pods

Small, invite-based groups that feel more like a group chat than a forum. Leaderboards rank consistency against goals you set yourself, never raw puff counts, so a quitter and a tracker can share a pod without being compared.

03

Equal pathways

Red pill or blue pill at onboarding, switchable any time from Profile. Your data carries over and the app re-skins around you. Autonomy is the retention mechanic.

Business model

The module is the only purchase. The app stays free, closer to the Oura or Whoop model than a subscription quit program. Per-unit hardware cost projects well under $25 at volume, and campus ambassadors are the first growth channel.

05 · System + information architecture

How it connects

The interface and the hardware were built in parallel by different people, so we froze a data contract early and treated it as the source of truth. The module sends two kinds of events. The app derives every number from them, which means no chart in the product is hand-entered or hardcoded.

Pressure sensorMPRLS · reads each draw
→
ESP32-C3count · duration · time
→
BLE linkbuffers, syncs in bursts
→
Derivation layerevery chart computed live
→
Home · Podswhat people see
// Event A · puff · sent after each draw
session_id     42
timestamp      ISO UTC, module clock
duration_ms    2100
intensity      0.68 relative, never mg
device_battery 0.83
// Event B · session_summary · at cap close
session_id    42
start / end   ISO UTC
puff_count    4
total_draw_ms 8300

Events buffer while your phone is away and land in one burst when you reconnect, so late data still has to fall into the right hour on the heat map. That changed what friction meant. It was no longer logging, it was trust that the numbers are current, so a visible sync pill made it into the header.

Retention loop

The daily Exhale

01Random-time snapshot
→
02Exhale notification
→
03Your daily reveal
→
04Pod leaderboard
→
05Share or go quiet
↺

Since logging is automatic, the daily trigger couldn't be "log your vape." Instead, once a day at an unpredictable time, Exhale freezes that day's data into a snapshot and pulls you back in to see where you landed on your pod's leaderboard, which refreshes every 24 hours. Sharing is on by default, and a "quiet today" toggle opts you out for a single day without making you press share every morning.

06 · Iteration process

From sketch to screen

Structure first, atmosphere last. I moved through four stages, and each one had a different job: paper to argue about structure, grayscale to argue about hierarchy, three visual directions to argue about brand, and high fidelity to prove it all held together with real data.

01

Sketches + user flows

Weeks 0 to 1 · paper, black and white only

I started on paper with user flows for the stats view and the friend pod, then drew a carousel of every tab so the team could argue about structure before anyone argued about color. The hardest question was how to move between pods. I sketched a focus pod at center screen with other pods fading in and out in 3D as you scroll, like switching group chats. Meisum sketched an all-in-one bubble: swipe up and down to change pods, left and right through your own stats, long press for the group. We merged the two, then added small directional cue bubbles that appear the moment you start dragging, so the gesture map teaches itself.

Concept A · Caroline

Focus pod scroll

Concept B · Meisum

All-in-one bubble

Shipped direction

Merged: bubble + cues

02

Grayscale wireframes

Weeks 2 to 3 · iOS spec, no color allowed

Wireframes stayed grayscale on purpose. Without color, I could catch a screen leaning judgmental through emphasis alone, a heavier number or a shrinking bar, before a palette had the chance to disguise it. Everything was built to iOS spec: 393 x 852 frames, 16pt margins, an 8pt vertical rhythm, 44pt minimum tap targets, and an 83pt tab bar.

Profile

Home and Stats merged

Adamaris flagged they were the same screen twice. Now the app opens to a calm ring and one tap reveals day, week and month.

Progressive disclosure

The minimal ring is the default read. Heat map, bars and trends appear only when you ask for them, which keeps cognitive load low on a stigmatized topic.

Leaderboard lives in the pod

You only ever see your own individual numbers. Everyone else shows up as a rank, so nobody is compared puff for puff.

03

Three visual directions

Weeks 4 to 5 · tested against our non-negotiables

With structure locked, I pushed three looks and judged each one against the rule we'd written into the product spec: never glamorize vaping. The brand had to feel like a social app people want to open, without ever making the device look cool.

A · Neon Glass

Cut

Lime glow and a glass prism wrapped around the device. Strong Matrix energy, but it turned the vape into the hero object and read like a product ad.

B · Warm Signal

Cut

A coral to blue gradient, softer and friendlier. The dashed calm ring was born here. It drifted toward wellness app, the exact positioning we'd decided to leave.

C · Iridescent Dark

Shipped

A near-black base with soft, blurred gradient bubbles and no hard outlines. Calm without being clinical, social without being loud.

04

High fidelity

Weeks 5 to 8 · dark base everywhere, bright accents only where data lives

The final system keeps the dark base on every screen and saves its brightest accents for stats, where color has a real job: showing intensity without judging it. Pods and settings stay quiet so the social layer never feels like a feed you have to keep up with.

Color describes intensity, never morality.

The ramp runs from quiet teal to warm ember. There are no red failure states anywhere in the app, so a heavy Friday night reads as information instead of a grade. Shown here with sample data.

Principles

Rules every screen follows

Bubbles, never boxes

Gradient shapes with no hard outlines, always in slow motion.

Mono for data

Numbers are the hero. Labels stay small and muted.

Judgment-free copy

"6 under your limit, nice." Never "you failed." "Logged," never "caught."

No glamor

No flavor ratings, no "cloud" or "haze" naming, no product shots of a vape.

Accessible by default

44pt tap targets and high-contrast celery text on a near-black base.

Customizable, within reason

Users can recolor outlines like ambient lighting in a car. The dark base never changes.

08 · Hardware · in progress

Where the data comes from

The interface is demo-ready. The physical module is still in calibration. Meisum leads hardware. My side is making sure the interface is ready for real data the moment it's trustworthy, and that nothing on screen promises more precision than the sensor can deliver.

Slip-on collar + side pod

Recommended

A stretchy silicone collar fits most vapes. A side pod holds the ESP32-C3, a 150 mAh LiPo and USB-C charging.

Inline pass-through

Best signal

Air passes straight through a central bore past an inline sensor. The cleanest reading, but it adds 2 to 3 cm of length.

Low-profile ring

Smallest

Everything packed into a flat ring. The cleanest look, and the hardest place to fit a battery.

Module concepts and build by Meisum. Parts: QT Py ESP32-C3, MPRLS ported pressure sensor, LiPo charger, reed switches for cap-open wake, platinum-cure silicone.

Build status

Where it stands

Jul

Parts sourced and the first standalone module assembled.

Aug

The Bluetooth link to a computer worked, and the sensor caught real hits accurately.

Aug 27

The sensor started drifting. We're reordering the same part and testing an alternative supplier in parallel.

Next

A 30 to 40 hit calibration test across different draw lengths, then a bulk order of 5 to 10 units.

Statistical analysis

Open questions

Where heavy begins

Research points to daily vs. non-daily as the strongest single line, with 200+ puffs a day as a heavy marker. In-app thresholds stay basic until our own data sets the benchmark.

Intensity is relative

The sensor reports draw depth from 0 to 1, so the interface never presents it as milligrams.

Cost is an estimate

Money and nicotine figures come from a price you enter at onboarding, and they're always labeled that way.

Built to swap

The front end runs on a mock Bluetooth adapter that emits contract-shaped events, so plugging in the real module is a one-line change.

09 · Reflection

End results + next steps

What worked

The bones held

The structure survived every visual pass. The gray Home and the iridescent Home share the same bones: a greeting, a ring, and one tap to depth. That told me the wireframe work did its job, and the visual layer could earn its atmosphere without adding complexity. Holding both personas against every decision also kept the product honest. Whenever a feature quietly started favoring quitters, the blue pill test caught it.

What I'd change

Test with real vapers sooner

Our personas came from secondary research and our own circles. The questions we still have, like how often the daily prompt should fire and what "heavy" should mean on screen, are ones only usability testing can answer. Next round, real users get in front of the wireframes before the visual pass, not after.

Roadmap

Next steps

01

Calibrate the module and complete the first end-to-end data round trip on a phone

02

Run usability tests with 5 to 8 vapers 21+, split evenly across both pathways

03

Design onboarding: pathway choice, device pairing, cost entry, and day-one empty states

04

Test a daily reflective prompt drawn from a content bank before locking notification cadence

05

Move to a native Bluetooth build, since Web Bluetooth doesn't run in iOS Safari

The point was never to make anyone quit. It was to let people see the pattern clearly, then trust them with what happens next.
